[CH01 | 0:00–1:30 | 冷开场:先摆一件看得见的文件级物证,再当场揭晓观众默认的因果是反的,登记主问题,并同时打开三条不作回答的悬念]

Calcutta. A council chamber. On the table, a law two paragraphs long.

Passed June 20, 1837. In force that December.

Read it and it barely sounds like anything. From that day, the government may waive the rule that court papers and tax papers be written in Persian. And whichever language replaces it? That gets named later. By the government.

Here is what those two paragraphs cancelled. Not some foreign tongue nobody used. That was the language Indian offices had been run in for centuries — the same year, the East India Company declared English the official language in Bengal, and Persian was swept out of the courts and the revenue offices entirely.

One signature. A whole working language, gone from the machinery it ran.

And the reach of that machinery is the part that doesn't add up. Historians have a name for it — the Persianate world, from the Balkans all the way to Bengal. Not Persia. Something much wider than Persia. One qualifier before we go on, because it matters for everything after: this was a written language of courts and administration. Not what people spoke at home. Nobody's mother tongue. Offices.

Now the strange part. The homeland of that language, during the centuries it covered the most ground, had no Persian empire of its own. None. A place that kept losing wars.

So how did it ever reach Bengal? Who actually laid that map down, if not Persia?

You've heard the explanation. Everyone who conquered Iran ended up becoming Persian. People still repeat it — in print, this year.

Somewhere in that sentence, the arrow is pointing the wrong way.

And in a courthouse in Bengal, a clerk who read and wrote for a living is about to find out what it costs.

[CH02 | 1:30–4:30 | 把主体退回最低点:交代它差点彻底消失、靠什么活下来,再揭示它真正可卖的能力不是文学而是公文手艺,并用一个丢掉了自己古语言的地区做失败对照]

Before we find out who laid that map down, we have to look at what this language actually had in hand at its lowest point. It wasn't an army. This stretch decides who ends up working for whom for the next seven hundred years, so stay with me. Three questions. What survived the collapse. Who saved it. And what part of it was actually worth paying for — because those last two have different answers.

Question one. What was left.

The Arab conquests ran from 633 to 651. In 651 the last Sasanian king, Yazdegerd III, was killed, and the empire that had run the Iranian plateau was simply gone. Arabic moved into the official rooms and the religious ones. The language of the old administration was pushed out of both. Not banned into silence, just demoted — which, for a written language, amounts to the same thing. No court writes in it. No treasury keeps accounts in it. A written language with no office to work in has roughly a generation before nobody can write it well.

Look at Egypt if you want to see how that story usually ends. Same conquest, same century, same pressure. Egypt lost its ancient language. Persian didn't. That's the puzzle of the next two centuries.

Question two. Who kept it alive.

By the ninth and tenth centuries the Samanid court was deliberately reviving New Persian — paying for it, writing in it, making it a thing a serious man could do. And the figure everyone points to is a poet. Ferdowsi. According to the standard accounts, he spent roughly thirty years on the *Shahnameh*, finished around the year 1010, somewhere between fifty and sixty thousand couplets, written on purpose in Persian. Scholars still describe him, in those words, as the man who saved the Persian language.

Thirty years. One writing life, spent giving a language a reason to still exist.

There's a story about how he was paid, from a biography written about a hundred and fifty years later, so treat it as a story and not a record. The sultan had promised a gold coin per couplet. What arrived was silver. Ferdowsi took the silver to a bathhouse and handed it out to the attendant and the water-seller. By the time the gold was finally on its way, the money entering the city by one gate met the poet's funeral leaving by another. Legend, probably. But it tells you something true: he knew he hadn't got what he was promised.

Now the part most people stop before.

Here's the thing about poetry. It doesn't pay a salary. The *Shahnameh* kept Persian alive. It didn't put it in Bengal.

What put it in Bengal was the unglamorous half of the same written tradition. Across its long life — old, middle, new — written Persian had produced something a poem can't produce: a stable class of scribes whose main job description, according to an Oxford University Press volume on the subject, wasn't literature at all. It was administration. Archives. Tax registers. Appointment papers. Court correspondence. The paperwork a state dies without.

And they didn't just serve one state. These were professionals who ran the documents of courts across Eurasia — from Mongol-ruled East Asia all the way to the Ottoman Balkans. Not as a people with a homeland to defend. As a trade, with a skill set, available for hire.

So: what survived 651 was a written language, and a profession. The language is the part everyone remembers. The profession is the part that got bought.

Which raises the only question that matters next. If this was a service, somebody had to be the first to pay for it. Who was the first customer?

[CH03 | 4:30–7:30 | 引入真正的使用方作为第二主角,用一个极具体的偶然说明采用的原因不是崇拜而是不得已,并打开两条留到后段才收的悬念]

The first customer was not a reader. He was a commander who had just taken a province and discovered, about a week later, that a province is mostly paperwork.

That is the whole second half of this story. From the tenth century onward, the men winning the battles across the Iranian plateau and Khurasan were mostly Turkic — slave-soldiers who rose, then generals, then dynasties. They could take a city in a season. What they could not do was assess its farmland, collect its taxes, record its land titles, keep its correspondence, and do all of that in a script their own commanders could not write. So they did what anyone with territory and no filing system does. They hired.

And here is where the whole thing stops being majestic and starts being almost embarrassingly small.

Take the court at Ghazna, the Turkic power that pushed east into northern India. Mahmud, its most famous ruler. For roughly the first ten or eleven years of his reign, the administration of that court ran in Persian — not Arabic, which was the prestige language of religion, law and learning across the entire Islamic world at the time. Why? According to an older Persian-language study of the period, the reason was his vizier. A man named Abu'l-Abbas Fazl b. Ahmad. And Abu'l-Abbas Fazl b. Ahmad could not read Arabic.

That's it. That's the policy.

Then the job changed hands. A new vizier came in, Maymandi, who was perfectly comfortable in Arabic — and Arabic came back into the chancery. One appointment out, one appointment in, and the official written language of an expanding empire flipped with it.

Remember this man. He comes back later in this story, and when he does, he settles the argument.

Because notice what that tells you. Nobody at Ghazna had been overwhelmed by the beauty of Persian poetry and converted. The court was running both languages side by side — a review in an academic journal of the standard history of the Ghaznavids treats the bilingual chancery under Mahmud's son Mas'ud as the moment New Persian had reached full parity with Arabic in affairs of state in the eastern Iranian world. Both were on the shelf. Which one got used came down to who was holding the post.

Which opens a question I'm going to leave open for a while: if an empire adopts this language because of a staffing gap, then what is actually being bought here? Not a culture. Something narrower than that.

Now the part that genuinely should not make sense.

Move west, two generations on. The Seljuks tear into Anatolia and take it off the Byzantines — brand new ground, nobody's inherited bureaucracy, a clean sheet. Their own language is Turkic. The language on the ground is Greek. The language of the faith is Arabic. Three obvious options.

They designated Persian. The Seljuk rulers and their Anatolian branch installed it as the language of administration, and in Konya, their capital, Persian was the common tongue of the place — that's the finding in several studies of Anatolian Seljuk administration and literary culture, including work in a journal of Iranian studies. Conquerors in freshly taken land, using none of the three languages you'd expect, and running the state in a fourth they brought in from outside.

And this is not an inference from poems. A paper published by the Turkish Historical Society describes surviving appointment documents from the reign of Alp Arslan — including one handing the governorship of Khwarazm to one of his sons. The paperwork by which a Seljuk sultan appointed his own child to a province is in Persian.

So by now it's not a favor to one vizier. It's how states get run. Which leaves one thing unexplained — two, actually. How does a system this deeply installed ever get cancelled by a few lines on a page? Hold that.

And first: an accident can happen to anyone. Who turned this one into something nobody could pull back out?

[CH04 | 7:30–9:50 | 把上一章的偶然做成制度:给出一份把自己嵌进客户国家机器的动作清单,并交出第一组同口径的扩张量级]

One man: Nizam al-Mulk.

He started under Chaghri Beg — one of the Seljuk founders. When Alp Arslan took power, Nizam al-Mulk became his vizier. Alp Arslan faced rivals. Nizam al-Mulk crushed them. The throne stabilized.

Then Alp Arslan died. The question was who would succeed him. Nizam al-Mulk picked Malikshah — Alp Arslan's son — and made sure he got the throne. Malikshah kept Nizam al-Mulk on as vizier. Gave him the title Atabak.

Nizam al-Mulk served roughly ten years under Alp Arslan. Then he carried on under Malikshah. Total run as vizier: about thirty years — from around 1064 to 1092. Scholars call him the chief architect of Seljuk administration.

Here's what that means. He didn't just advise rulers. He built the bureaucratic structure they ruled through. Tax collection. Record keeping. Appointments. The whole apparatus. And the people staffing it — the Persian scribes, the Persian clerks — were bound to the Seljuk state.

When the Seljuks expanded, those officials went with them. New territory meant new tax rolls, new courts, new administration. And all of it ran in Persian. The Seljuks were the military. The Persian administrative class was the infrastructure. You couldn't separate one from the other.

So what happened? Wherever Seljuk power reached, Persian as an administrative language followed.

Take Anatolia. The Seljuks took it from the Byzantines starting in 463 AH — 1081. After that, Persian remained the official and administrative language there for over five centuries. In major cities, it was the working language. In the madrasas — the academies — it was taught as a subject. In official correspondence, it was the preferred script.

In Konya — capital of the Rum Seljuks — Persian was the common administrative tongue. Not Turkish. Not Greek. Not Arabic. Persian.

And this wasn't about one generation of rulers loving Persian poetry. This was structural. The bureaucracy was Persian-speaking. The tax system was Persian-speaking. The legal records were Persian-speaking. Once it was installed, it didn't matter which sultan came next. The machinery kept running in the same language.

Which brings the count to: one region, five centuries, embedded in government training and official communication.

But Anatolia's just one stop. The question now is: how much further east could this system stretch — and how many more clients would pay for it?

[CH05 | 9:50–13:30 | 把覆盖量级连续升级到观众原以为不可能的程度,同时坦白主体自身的硬限定却给出继续扩张的反向结果,并回收开场那件物证、第一次正面触到片名]

The answer is: all the way across two continents — and through three completely different sets of clients.

Before we see how far, let me ask you this. Think about the layer of your work that you use every day but would never build yourself. The protocols. The templates. The software everyone in your field just assumes is there. That's what we're talking about. A system people rent, not own.

Now watch what happens when the clients change clothes but keep hiring the same scribes.

First stop: the steppe empires, the ones that rode in on horseback and brought a new religion with them. In 1295, the Ilkhanate's Mahmud Ghazan converted to Islam. That move made Mongol rule acceptable to his Muslim subjects — and it opened the door to a cultural boom. He funded artists. He funded scholars. And under his sponsorship, Rashid al-Din Hamadani completed the first true world history, written in Persian.

Scholars today describe what happened next as a "double rapprochement" — a two-way convergence, not a one-way surrender. The Mongol elite didn't become Persian. One signature. A whole working language, gone from the machinery it ran.

Now the strange part. The homeland of that language, during the centuries it covered the most ground, had no Persian empire of its own. None. A place that kept losing wars.

So how did it ever reach Bengal? Who actually laid that map down, if not Persia?

You've heard the explanation. Everyone who conquered Iran ended up becoming Persian. People still repeat it.

Somewhere in that sentence, the arrow is pointing the wrong way.

Before we find out who laid that map down, we have to look at what this language actually had at its lowest point. This stretch decides who ends up working for whom for the next seven hundred years. Question one. What was left.

The Arab conquests ran from 633 to 651. In 651 the last Sasanian king was killed, and the empire that had run the Iranian plateau was simply gone. Arabic moved into the official rooms and the religious ones. The language of the old administration was pushed out. A written language with no office to work in has roughly a generation before nobody can write it well.

Look at Egypt if you want to see how that story usually ends. Same conquest, same century, same pressure. Egypt lost its ancient language. Persian didn't.

Question two. Who kept it alive.

By the ninth and tenth centuries the Samanid court was deliberately reviving New Persian. And the figure everyone points to is a poet. Ferdowsi. He spent roughly thirty years on the *Shahnameh*, finished around 1010, somewhere between fifty and sixty thousand couplets, written on purpose in Persian. Scholars still describe him as the man who saved the Persian language.

Thirty years. One writing life, spent giving a language a reason to still exist.

There's a story about how he was paid, from a biography written about a hundred and fifty years later, so treat it as a story. The sultan had promised a gold coin per couplet. What arrived was silver. Ferdowsi took the silver to a bathhouse and handed it out. By the time the gold was finally on its way, the money entering the city by one gate met the poet's funeral leaving by another. Legend, probably. But it tells you something true: he knew he hadn't got what he was promised.

Now the part most people stop before.

Poetry doesn't pay a salary. The *Shahnameh* kept Persian alive. It didn't put it in Bengal.

What put it in Bengal was the unglamorous half of the same written tradition. Written Persian had produced something a poem can't produce: a stable class of scribes whose main job, according to an Oxford University Press volume, wasn't literature at all. It was administration. Archives. Tax registers. Appointment papers. Court correspondence. The paperwork a state dies without.

And they didn't just serve one state. These were professionals who ran the documents of courts across Eurasia — from Mongol-ruled East Asia all the way to the Ottoman Balkans. Not as a people with a homeland to defend. As a trade, with a skill set, available for hire.

So: what survived 651 was a written language, and a profession. The profession is the part that got bought.

But what could this system actually do? Tax assessment. Land registry. Court correspondence. Contract enforcement. Archive keeping. Every piece of paperwork a state needs to collect revenue and maintain order. And they weren't reinventing the wheel every time. There were standard forms. Standard procedures. Standard training. A Persian scribe trained in one court could walk into another and know exactly what to do.

The people who'd just conquered a province? They could fight. They couldn't file.

Which raises the only question that matters next. If this was a service, somebody had to be the first to pay for it. Who was the first customer?

The first customer was not a reader. He was a commander who had just taken a province and discovered that a province is mostly paperwork.

And here is where the whole thing stops being majestic.

Take the court at Ghazna. Mahmud, its most famous ruler. For roughly the first fifteen years of his reign, the administration ran in Persian — not Arabic, which was the prestige language of religion, law and learning across the Islamic world at the time. Why? According to an older Persian-language study, the reason was his vizier. A man named Abu'l-Abbas Fazl b. Ahmad. And Abu'l-Abbas Fazl b. Ahmad could not read Arabic.

That's it. That's the policy.

Then the job changed hands. A new vizier came in, Maymandi, who was perfectly comfortable in Arabic — and Arabic came back into the chancery.

Pause on that. One appointment out, one appointment in, and the official written language of an expanding empire flipped with it. This isn't cultural magnetism. This is a staffing issue. One appointment out, one appointment in, and the official written language of an expanding empire flipped with it.

Remember this man. He comes back later, and when he does, he settles the argument.

Which opens a question: if an empire adopts this language because of a staffing gap, then what is actually being bought here?

stale_facts.content: John Perry 的判断:从加兹尼与塞尔柱往后，大多数伊朗政权的突厥语统治者本身已经被伊朗化并在自己领地内赞助波斯文学，因此突厥人统治的帝国扩张，等于把书面波斯语的版图扩张到被征服地区，尤其是安纳托利亚、中亚与南亚。
大约从公元十一世纪起，新波斯语成为北方与东方伊斯兰世界几乎所有非阿拉伯语口语地区宫廷精英的书面文学语言，这个局面至少延续到十八世纪，之后还留有明显痕迹。
波斯语在安纳托利亚做了五个多世纪的官方与行政语言;这个过程的第一阶段始于大塞尔柱于 463 AH 攻入拜占庭在该地区的领土。

stale_facts.content: Mahmud of Ghazna 在位的头十到十一年行政语言是波斯语，原因是他的宰相 Abu'l-Abbas Fazl b. Ahmad 不懂阿拉伯语;换上通晓阿拉伯语的 Maymandi 之后阿拉伯语又回到朝廷。
Nizam al-Mulk 先到 Chaghri Beg 帐下，后任 Alp Arslan 宰相、镇压对手稳住其统治;Alp Arslan 死后扶 Malikshah 上位并继任宰相、获 Atabak 称号;总共掌宰相位约三十年，是塞尔柱统治的主要行政设计者。波斯官员与塞尔柱的紧密绑定，使波斯语随塞尔柱势力所及而扩散。
英国统治确立后，1837 年英语取代波斯语成为印度行政的官方语言，并推行英语与印度本地语言的教育;Macaulay 1835 年的印度教育备忘录被普遍视为这一决策背后观点的代表。
英国统治在印度确立后波斯语不再是官方语言，1837 年被从官署中清除;同年东印度公司在孟加拉宣布英语为官方语言。
Act No. XXIX of 1837(《司法与税务程序语言法》)于 1837 年 6 月 20 日由印度参事会通过，自 1837 年 12 月 1 日起生效:授权印度总督参事会以参事会令的形式，普遍地或在其认为合适的地方范围内，免除孟加拉法典中任何要求在司法程序或税务程序中使用波斯语的规定，并规定此类程序中应使用的语言与字体。该法后于 1874 年由 Act 16 of 1874 废止。
1844 年 Hardinge 发布公告，政府职员的选任此后只依据英语知识和接受过的英语教育。

学界明确反对把 Indo-Persian 的衰亡只归于殖民语言政策。Brill 该章(第 8 章 'The Antipodes of "Progress": A Journey to the End of Indo-Persian')指出，以往用 Cohn 的「语言的统治」或 Tariq Rahman 的「波斯语失去权力也就失去声望」来解释「太简单了」:很多印度语言在殖民语言政策下照样活了下来，最典型的是同样被排挤的旁遮普语;真正原因还包括 Indo-Persian 自身在审美与知识上的保守化，印度知识人不愿再绑在一门比本地语言更僵化的文学媒介上——用作者的话说，它「成了自己过去的囚徒」。

1206 年德里苏丹国建立后，波斯语成为印度次大陆的行政语言;孟加拉 1203/04 年被征服后，波斯语被用于全部行政、文学与经济领域，钱币也用波斯文铸刻。莫卧儿 1526 年建国，阿克巴 1556 年即位后改革币制，把孟加拉地区钱币的铭文从阿拉伯文改为波斯文。从阿克巴即位到 Mohammad Shah 去世(1556–1749)的两百年莫卧儿统治，给整个北印度和部分德干带来了统一的官方语言、行政体系与币制。
波斯语在德干数世纪里是行政、外交与档案的主要语言:贵族与官员受训时用马拉提语管军政、用波斯语做外交与对帝国的交涉、用梵语处理法律与礼制;Shivaji 的往来文书显示他熟悉波斯外交惯例，同时用马拉提语向军事与税务官员下令。具体文书层面:一份 18 世纪下半叶的手稿藏品里，存有一封用波斯语写给法国国王、谈印度对英战争(德干的 Nāzim、本地治里之围等)的信件副本。
土耳其历史学会(TTK)的论文介绍了大塞尔柱苏丹 Alp Arslan(1063–1072)时期的几份波斯语任命文书(tayin mengûru)，抄自 Alp Arslan 时代的文书集《Tarassul-i Bahā'ī》;其中一份是 Alp Arslan 把下属花剌子模省的治理权授予他某个儿子的任命文书。
阿拉伯征服 633—651 年;末代萨珊王耶兹德格德三世 651 年被杀，波斯语在官方与宗教场合被阿拉伯语压制。九至十世纪萨曼王朝宫廷复兴新波斯语;菲尔多西耗时约 30 年完成《列王纪》(约 1010 年成书，5 万—6 万联句)，刻意用波斯语书写，被公认为「拯救了波斯语」。对照组:埃及在阿拉伯化过程中丢掉了古埃及语，波斯语没有。
1837 年取消波斯语之后，替代语言由政府逐地指定，并不都是英语:奥里萨方面，税务高等委员会(Sudder Board of Revenue)1837 年决定在公署停止使用波斯语，随后部分官员主张应改用孟加拉语、另一部分主张印度斯坦语，由此起了争执;1838 年若干本地语言获得官方承认。当时的参事会记录亦承认，骤然更换公务语言会在许多地区造成严重的公共不便，并使许多长期服务的旧吏陷入困境。

versions.text:
# Optimized Script

[CH01 | 0:00–1:30 | 冷开场:先摆一件看得见的文件级物证,再当场揭晓观众默认的因果是反的,登记主问题,并同时打开三条不作回答的悬念]

Calcutta. A council chamber. On the table, a law that says the government may waive the rule that court papers and tax papers be written in Persian. And whichever language replaces it? That gets named later.

Passed in 1837. In force that December.

Here is what those two paragraphs cancelled. Not some foreign tongue nobody used. That was the language Indian offices had been run in for centuries. The same year, the East India Company declared English the official language in Bengal, and Persian was swept out entirely.

One signature. A whole working language, gone from the machinery it ran.

And the reach of that machinery is the part that doesn't add up. Historians call it the Persianate world, from the Balkans all the way to Bengal. Not Persia. Something much wider. One qualifier: this was a written language of courts and administration. Not what people spoke at home. Offices.

Now the strange part. The homeland of that language, during the centuries it covered the most ground, had no Persian empire of its own. None. A place that kept losing wars.

So how did it ever reach Bengal? Who actually laid that map down, if not Persia?

You've heard the explanation. Everyone who conquered Iran ended up becoming Persian. People still repeat it.

Somewhere in that sentence, the arrow is pointing the wrong way.

[CH02 | 1:30–4:30 | 把主体退回最低点:交代它差点彻底消失、靠什么活下来,再揭示它真正可卖的能力不是文学而是公文手艺,并用一个丢掉了自己古语言的地区做失败对照]

Before we find out who laid that map down, we have to look at what this language actually had at its lowest point. This stretch decides who ends up working for whom for the next seven hundred years. Three questions. What survived the collapse. Who saved it. And what part of it was actually worth paying for.

Question one. What was left.

The Arab conquests ran from 633 to 651. In 651 the last Sasanian king was killed, and the empire that had run the Iranian plateau was simply gone. Arabic moved into the official rooms and the religious ones. The language of the old administration was pushed out. A written language with no office to work in has roughly a generation before nobody can write it well.

Look at Egypt if you want to see how that story usually ends. Same conquest, same century, same pressure. Egypt lost its ancient language. Persian didn't.

Question two. Who kept it alive.

By the ninth and tenth centuries the Samanid court was deliberately reviving New Persian. And the figure everyone points to is a poet. Ferdowsi. He spent roughly thirty years on the *Shahnameh*, finished around 1010, somewhere between fifty and sixty thousand couplets, written on purpose in Persian. Scholars still describe him as the man who saved the Persian language.

Thirty years. One writing life, spent giving a language a reason to still exist.

There's a story about how he was paid, from a biography written about a hundred and fifty years later, so treat it as a story. The sultan had promised a gold coin per couplet. What arrived was silver. Ferdowsi took the silver to a bathhouse and handed it out. By the time the gold was finally on its way, the money entering the city by one gate met the poet's funeral leaving by another. Legend, probably. But it tells you something true: he knew he hadn't got what he was promised.

Now the part most people stop before.

Poetry doesn't pay a salary. The *Shahnameh* kept Persian alive. It didn't put it in Bengal.

What put it in Bengal was the unglamorous half of the same written tradition. Written Persian had produced something a poem can't produce: a stable class of scribes whose main job, according to an Oxford University Press volume, wasn't literature at all. It was administration. Archives. Tax registers. Appointment papers. Court correspondence. The paperwork a state dies without.

And they didn't just serve one state. These were professionals who ran the documents of courts across Eurasia — from Mongol-ruled East Asia all the way to the Ottoman Balkans. Not as a people with a homeland to defend. As a trade, with a skill set, available for hire.

So: what survived 651 was a written language, and a profession. The profession is the part that got bought.

Which raises the only question that matters next. If this was a service, somebody had to be the first to pay for it. Who was the first customer?

[CH03 | 4:30–7:30 | 引入真正的使用方作为第二主角,用一个极具体的偶然说明采用的原因不是崇拜而是不得已,并打开两条留到后段才收的悬念]

The first customer was not a reader. He was a commander who had just taken a province and discovered that a province is mostly paperwork.

From the tenth century onward, the men winning the battles across the Iranian plateau were mostly Turkic — slave-soldiers who rose, then generals, then dynasties. They could take a city in a season. What they could not do was assess its farmland, collect its taxes, record its land titles, keep its correspondence. So they did what anyone with territory and no filing system does. They hired.

And here is where the whole thing stops being majestic.

Take the court at Ghazna. Mahmud, its most famous ruler. For roughly the first ten or eleven years of his reign, the administration ran in Persian — not Arabic, which was the prestige language of religion, law and learning across the Islamic world at the time. Why? According to an older Persian-language study, the reason was his vizier. A man named Abu'l-Abbas Fazl b. Ahmad. And Abu'l-Abbas Fazl b. Ahmad could not read Arabic.

That's it. That's the policy.

Then the job changed hands. A new vizier came in, Maymandi, who was perfectly comfortable in Arabic — and Arabic came back into the chancery. One appointment out, one appointment in, and the official written language of an expanding empire flipped with it.

Remember this man. He comes back later, and when he does, he settles the argument.

Because notice what that tells you. Nobody at Ghazna had been overwhelmed by the beauty of Persian poetry. The court was running both languages side by side — a review treats the bilingual chancery under Mahmud's son Mas'ud as the moment New Persian had reached full parity with Arabic in affairs of state. Both were on the shelf. Which one got used came down to who was holding the post.

Which opens a question: if an empire adopts this language because of a staffing gap, then what is actually being bought here?

Now the part that genuinely should not make sense.

Move west, two generations on. The Seljuks tear into Anatolia and take it off the Byzantines — brand new ground, nobody's inherited bureaucracy. Their own language is Turkic. The language on the ground is Greek. The language of the faith is Arabic. Three obvious options.

They designated Persian. The Seljuk rulers and their Anatolian branch installed it as the language of administration, and in Konya, their capital, Persian was the common tongue — that's the finding in several studies of Anatolian Seljuk administration. Conquerors in freshly taken land, using none of the three languages you'd expect.

And this is not an inference from poems. A paper published by the Turkish Historical Society describes surviving appointment documents from Alp Arslan — including one handing the governorship of Khwarazm to one of his sons. The paperwork by which a Seljuk sultan appointed his own child to a province is in Persian.

So by now it's not a favor to one vizier. It's how states get run. Which leaves one thing unexplained. How does a system this deeply installed ever get cancelled by a few lines on a page? Hold that.

And first: who turned this accident into something nobody could pull back out?

[CH04 | 7:30–9:50 | 把上一章的偶然做成制度:给出一份把自己嵌进客户国家机器的动作清单,并交出第一组同口径的扩张量级]

One man: Nizam al-Mulk.

He started under Chaghri Beg — one of the Seljuk founders. When Alp Arslan took power, Nizam al-Mulk became his vizier. Alp Arslan faced rivals. Nizam al-Mulk crushed them. The throne stabilized.

Then Alp Arslan died. Nizam al-Mulk picked Malikshah — Alp Arslan's son — and made sure he got the throne. Malikshah kept Nizam al-Mulk on as vizier. Total run: about thirty years — from around 1064 to 1092. Scholars call him the chief architect of Seljuk administration.

He didn't just advise rulers. He built the bureaucratic structure they ruled through. Tax collection. Record keeping. Appointments. The whole apparatus. And the people staffing it — the Persian scribes, the Persian clerks — were bound to the Seljuk state. When the Seljuks expanded, those officials went with them. New territory meant new tax rolls, new courts, new administration. And all of it ran in Persian.

The Seljuks were the military. The Persian administrative class was the infrastructure.

So what happened? Wherever Seljuk power reached, Persian as an administrative language followed.

Take Anatolia. The Seljuks took it from the Byzantines starting in 1081. After that, Persian remained the official and administrative language there for over five centuries. In major cities, it was the working language. In the madrasas it was taught as a subject. In official correspondence, it was the preferred script.

In Konya — capital of the Rum Seljuks — Persian was the common administrative tongue. Not Turkish. Not Greek. Not Arabic. Persian.

This wasn't about one generation of rulers loving Persian poetry. This was structural. The bureaucracy was Persian-speaking. The tax system was Persian-speaking. Once it was installed, it didn't matter which sultan came next. The machinery kept running in the same language.

Which brings the count to: one region, five centuries, embedded in government training and official communication.

But Anatolia's just one stop. The question now is: how much further east could this system stretch?

[CH05 | 9:50–13:30 | 把覆盖量级连续升级到观众原以为不可能的程度,同时坦白主体自身的硬限定却给出继续扩张的反向结果,并回收开场那件物证、第一次正面触到片名]

The answer is: all the way across two continents — and through three completely different sets of clients.

Think about the layer your field uses every day but never builds. That's what we're talking about.

Now watch what happens when the clients change clothes but keep hiring the same scribes.

First stop: the steppe empires. In 1295, the Ilkhanate's Mahmud Ghazan converted to Islam. That move made Mongol rule acceptable to his Muslim subjects. He funded scholars. And under his sponsorship, Rashid al-Din Hamadani completed the first true world history, written in Persian. Same scribes. New empire.

Second stop: the Indian subcontinent. In 1206, the Delhi Sultanate made Persian the administrative language. When Bengal was conquered in 1203 or 1204, Persian was used for all administration, all literature, all economic records. The coins were stamped in Persian script.

Then in 1556, Akbar took the throne. He reformed the currency. He changed the inscriptions on Bengal's coins from Arabic to Persian script. For the next two hundred years — from Akbar's accession to Mohammad Shah's death in 1749 — Mughal rule brought a unified official language, a unified administrative structure, and a unified coinage system to all of northern India.

And the Mughal Empire itself was founded by Persianized Turks from Central Asia. The people who built it had already been shaped by this administrative culture.

Third stop: even further out. In the Deccan, Persian remained the main language of administration, diplomacy, and record-keeping for centuries. Nobles were trained in three languages: Marathi for military and tax matters, Persian for diplomacy, Sanskrit for law and ritual.

And we have proof of just how far this system traveled. In a manuscript collection from the eighteenth century, there's a copy of a letter written in Persian to the king of France. It discusses the war against the British in India. A letter from one side of the world to the other, written in a language whose homeland hadn't controlled an empire of its own in centuries.

So let's reset the count. From the eleventh century onward, New Persian was the written literary language of the court elite in nearly all non-Arabic-speaking regions of the northern and eastern Islamic world. That position lasted at least until the eighteenth century. It stretched from the Balkans under the Ottomans all the way to Bengal under the Mughals.

But here's what we have to be honest about. This entire sprawl was never a language that ordinary people spoke at home. It was a written language of courts and government offices. It lived in tax ledgers and royal decrees, not in marketplaces. The people who could read and write it were a specialized class whose job was administration.

And that specialization is exactly what made it expandable. A language that ordinary people speak spreads with migration and conquest. A language that only administrators use spreads with whoever hires administrators.

Which brings us back to that table in Calcutta. That law passed on June twentieth, eighteen thirty-seven. In effect December first. The one that said the government could waive the requirement that court and tax documents be written in Persian — and decide later which language would replace it.

What those two paragraphs cancelled wasn't just a foreign tongue. It was a language Indian offices had used for centuries. A language that had travelled from the Balkans to Bengal not because Iran won wars, but because people who did win wars needed someone to run the bureaucracy they'd just conquered.

And that's the first time the title starts to make sense. Persian wasn't really a Persian language. It was a bureaucratic infrastructure. A system empires rented when they didn't have one of their own.

But if it was that useful, if it kept expanding for centuries — then why did it disappear?

[CH06 | 13:30–15:00 | 用一句重定义把前面所有扩张的归因整体掀翻,在同一处集中收掉前面积压的几条悬念,再开出最后一条]

So what was Persian actually selling?

The answer comes from a linguist who studied how this written language spread. John Perry looked at the Ghaznavids, the Seljuks, the Ilkhanids, the Mughals. He said: when their empires expanded, written Persian expanded with them. The conquests weren't Persian conquests.

In other words: the territory was someone else's victory. Persian was the hired help.

Now here's the part where everything you've heard gets flipped. There's a saying that still gets quoted — by Iranian state media, by Spanish newspaper columnists: "Everyone who conquered Persia eventually became Persian."

It sounds poetic. But it gets the direction backwards.

And remember that vizier in Ghazna who couldn't read Arabic? The one whose language gap made Persian the working language of the court for over a decade? When he was replaced, Arabic came right back. That's not cultural magnetism. That's a job someone can be fired from.

The poet who saved the language with thirty years and fifty to sixty thousand couplets — he kept it alive. But what kept it employed across the Balkans to Bengal, across Anatolia for over five centuries — that wasn't poetry. That was administrative capacity someone didn't want to build themselves.

Persian wasn't spreading because Iran kept winning. It was spreading because the people who did win needed accountants.

The timeline makes it obvious. The Iranian plateau had no Persian empire of its own for most of those centuries. But written Persian had its widest reach. The Seljuks brought it to Anatolia after taking the land from Byzantium — a place where they didn't use their own Turkic, didn't use the local Greek, didn't use Arabic. The Mughals brought it to Bengal. The Ilkhanids brought it into their administration. None of those were Persian armies. They were clients.

So the real business model wasn't representing a people. It was being the layer empires couldn't run without — and didn't want to build.

That's the answer to the question from the beginning. A country that kept losing wars still had its language spread to Bengal because the wars that mattered weren't its own. The conquerors weren't converting to a culture. They were hiring a system. And what got purchased was a skill set that could be dismissed.

Which brings us to the final question: if this system was that good, if it lasted that long — why did it end?

[CH07 | 15:00–17:25 | 主动把论点交给最不利的几条证据做压力测试,每条配一句不否认也不夸大的公允限定,论点不反转而是变窄变硬,并收掉一条早埋的悬念]

You've heard the version that makes it sound inevitable: Persian spread because everyone who conquered Iran became Persian. But the version you heard isn't complete.

First: the coverage itself. From the eleventh century through at least the eighteenth, New Persian was the written literary language of courtly elites in nearly all non-Arabic-speaking regions of the northern and eastern Islamic world. Notice what that sentence doesn't say. It doesn't say it was the language people spoke at home. This was an office language. It had users, but it didn't have a population that lived in it.

Second: the retreat started long before the British showed up. By the early sixteenth century, the rulers within the Persianate zone were already writing major works in their own tongues. Isma'il of the Safavids, Babur of the Mughals, Shaybani Khan of Bukhara — all composed in their native languages. Ottoman Turkish poetry had already developed its own tradition. When Ottoman forces took Tabriz in 1514, Persian literature briefly surged back. But starting in the 1530s, Turkish pushed it out. The decline was already three hundred years old by the time the 1837 document showed up.

Third: that document itself. Act No. XXIX of 1837 wasn't even a command to switch to English. It was an authorization. It allowed the government to waive the requirement that court and tax documents be written in Persian — and the replacement language would be designated by the government, province by province. In Orissa, the Board of Revenue stopped using Persian in 1837. Immediately, officials started arguing over whether to switch to Bengali or Hindustani. The following year, several local languages received official recognition. And the Council's own records admit that an abrupt change of language would cause serious public inconvenience and place many long-serving clerks in distress. They saw it coming. They did it anyway. What replaced Persian wasn't always English. Sometimes it was just whichever local language the government happened to pick.

Fourth: scholars who study this period explicitly reject the idea that you can blame it all on colonial policy. There's an academic volume published by Brill — one chapter is dedicated entirely to the end of Indo-Persian. The argument it makes is that the "language of rule" explanation is too simple. Because plenty of Indian languages survived under the same colonial language policies. The clearest example: Punjabi. It got pushed to the margins just like Persian did. Punjabi's still here. Indo-Persian isn't.

The difference: Punjabi had a population behind it. Persian had a client base. It didn't have a floor.

The chapter argues that Indo-Persian itself became aesthetically and intellectually conservative. Indian intellectuals didn't want to stay tied to a literary medium that had become more rigid than their own local languages. The phrase the author uses: it became "a prisoner of its own past."

That's the missing half. It didn't die because it lost a war. It had been losing ground for three centuries — not to conquest, but to the slow fact that no one needed to speak it at home. When the British wrote those two paragraphs, they weren't killing a culture. They were canceling a contract. And the contract could be canceled because what Persian sold was a service, not a root.

Which brings us to India. If the 1837 law was just the formal end, if the replacement language wasn't even settled — then who actually paid the cost when the office language changed?

[CH08 | 17:25–18:05 | 交出结局与代价账:把前面的制度性结论落到具体一群人身上,说明这个结局不可逆,收掉一条悬念并开出最后一条]

British India, 1830s. Macaulay's memo laid the ground. Then came 1837. That two-paragraph act. December 1st, Persian out.

The clerks who ran the lower courts and tax offices. Muslims had held those positions through 1837 — not because of favoritism, but because Persian was the language the system ran in.

For Hindu clerks who'd never used Persian at home, switching to English cost almost nothing. For the Muslim administrative class, it was a question of cultural identity — Persian had been the language of Muslim political elites. Their social and economic position collapsed.

Then 1844. Hardinge's order: government appointments from now on depend only on knowledge of English.

The council records from 1835 to '38 said it plainly: a sudden change of language would throw many longtime servants of the government into hardship. They knew. They went ahead anyway.

The system didn't lose a war. It lost the one thing it depended on: the job. No daily speakers to fall back on. When the platform got swapped out, everyone standing on it went down with it.

So what can you take from this?

[CH09 | 18:05–18:48 | 把全片压成几条编号法则,每条配一句机理,再给一组同口径对照和一句可被复述的终极句,并开出最后一个开放问题]

First: occupy the layer no one else wants to build. That scribal class didn't sell poetry. They sold the bureaucratic capacity an empire needs but can't staff on its own. Tax rolls. Edicts. Record keeping. That's what got bought.

Second: your distribution channel doesn't have to be your own. The Turkic conquests opened the territory. The Mongol campaigns opened more. Persian administrative language rode those victories from Anatolia to Bengal. It never won a battle. It got hired by the people who did.

And third: the ceiling isn't a battlefield. It's a procurement decision.

Here's what it took to build this system: from the eleventh century to the eighteenth, seven hundred years as the administrative language of courts across two continents. And what it took to cancel it: two paragraphs. Passed June 20, 1837. Effective December 1. The document didn't even name the replacement. Some provinces switched to local languages, not English.

Here's what you didn't hear in the usual version: it never depended on its own empire. It depended on someone else needing what it did. And the moment that changed, the system could be replaced by a memo that said, "to be determined by government order."

It never won on its own. It won because someone else won and couldn't run the place without it. And when the client picks a different contractor — even one no better than you — the old one just stops getting called.

One question: in your industry, what's the layer everyone uses but no one wants to build themselves?

[CH10 | 18:48–19:00 | 用一个不作回答的开放问题把结论交回观众自己的处境,并回扣开场那件物证收尾]

Calcutta. That council chamber. That table with two paragraphs on it.

Passed June 20, 1837. In effect December 1. The line that killed it: "the language to be used shall be such as the government may from time to time determine."

Not English. Not necessarily. Just: to be determined.

Next time you see a contract line that says "supplier to be designated by Party A," you'll remember those two paragraphs. You're either the product, or you're the platform under it. And platforms don't get defeated. They get redesignated.

[CH01 | 0:00–1:30 | 冷开场:先摆一件看得见的文件级物证,再当场揭晓观众默认的因果是反的,登记主问题,并同时打开三条不作回答的悬念]

Calcutta. A council chamber. On the table, a law that says the government may waive the rule that court papers and tax papers be written in Persian. And whichever language replaces it? That gets named later.

Passed in 1837. In force that December.

Here is what those two paragraphs cancelled. Not some foreign tongue nobody used. That was the language Indian offices had been run in for centuries. The same year, the East India Company declared English the official language in Bengal, and Persian was swept out entirely.

One signature. A whole working language, gone from the machinery it ran.

And the reach of that machinery is the part that doesn't add up. Historians call it the Persianate world, from the Balkans all the way to Bengal. Not Persia. Something much wider. One qualifier: this was a written language of courts and administration. Not what people spoke at home. Offices.

Now the strange part. The homeland of that language, during the centuries it covered the most ground, had no Persian empire of its own. None. A place that kept losing wars.

So how did it ever reach Bengal? Who actually laid that map down, if not Persia?

You've heard the explanation. Everyone who conquered Iran ended up becoming Persian. People still repeat it.

Somewhere in that sentence, the arrow is pointing the wrong way.

[CH02 | 1:30–4:30 | 把主体退回最低点:交代它差点彻底消失、靠什么活下来,再揭示它真正可卖的能力不是文学而是公文手艺,并用一个丢掉了自己古语言的地区做失败对照]

Before we find out who laid that map down, we have to look at what this language actually had at its lowest point. This stretch decides who ends up working for whom for the next seven hundred years. Three questions. What survived the collapse. Who saved it. And what part of it was actually worth paying for.

Question one. What was left.

The Arab conquests ran from 633 to 651. In 651 the last Sasanian king was killed, and the empire that had run the Iranian plateau was simply gone. Arabic moved into the official rooms and the religious ones. The language of the old administration was pushed out. A written language with no office to work in has roughly a generation before nobody can write it well.

Look at Egypt if you want to see how that story usually ends. Same conquest, same century, same pressure. Egypt lost its ancient language. Persian didn't.

Question two. Who kept it alive.

By the ninth and tenth centuries the Samanid court was deliberately reviving New Persian. And the figure everyone points to is a poet. Ferdowsi. He spent roughly thirty years on the *Shahnameh*, finished around 1010, somewhere between fifty and sixty thousand couplets, written on purpose in Persian. Scholars still describe him as the man who saved the Persian language.

Thirty years. One writing life, spent giving a language a reason to still exist.

There's a story about how he was paid, from a biography written about a hundred and fifty years later, so treat it as a story. The sultan had promised a gold coin per couplet. What arrived was silver. Ferdowsi took the silver to a bathhouse and handed it out. By the time the gold was finally on its way, the money entering the city by one gate met the poet's funeral leaving by another. Legend, probably. But it tells you something true: he knew he hadn't got what he was promised.

Now the part most people stop before.

Poetry doesn't pay a salary. The *Shahnameh* kept Persian alive. It didn't put it in Bengal.

What put it in Bengal was the unglamorous half of the same written tradition. Written Persian had produced something a poem can't produce: a stable class of scribes whose main job, according to an Oxford University Press volume, wasn't literature at all. It was administration. Archives. Tax registers. Appointment papers. Court correspondence. The paperwork a state dies without.

And they didn't just serve one state. These were professionals who ran the documents of courts across Eurasia — from Mongol-ruled East Asia all the way to the Ottoman Balkans. Not as a people with a homeland to defend. As a trade, with a skill set, available for hire.

So: what survived 651 was a written language, and a profession. The profession is the part that got bought.

Which raises the only question that matters next. If this was a service, somebody had to be the first to pay for it. Who was the first customer?

[CH03 | 4:30–7:30 | 引入真正的使用方作为第二主角,用一个极具体的偶然说明采用的原因不是崇拜而是不得已,并打开两条留到后段才收的悬念]

The first customer was not a reader. He was a commander who had just taken a province and discovered that a province is mostly paperwork.

From the tenth century onward, the men winning the battles across the Iranian plateau were mostly Turkic — slave-soldiers who rose, then generals, then dynasties. They could take a city in a season. What they could not do was assess its farmland, collect its taxes, record its land titles, keep its correspondence. So they did what anyone with territory and no filing system does. They hired.

And here is where the whole thing stops being majestic.

Take the court at Ghazna. Mahmud, its most famous ruler. For roughly the first fifteen years of his reign, the administration ran in Persian — not Arabic, which was the prestige language of religion, law and learning across the Islamic world at the time. Why? According to an older Persian-language study, the reason was his vizier. A man named Abu'l-Abbas Fazl b. Ahmad. And Abu'l-Abbas Fazl b. Ahmad could not read Arabic.

That's it. That's the policy.

Then the job changed hands. A new vizier came in, Maymandi, who was perfectly comfortable in Arabic — and Arabic came back into the chancery. One appointment out, one appointment in, and the official written language of an expanding empire flipped with it.

Remember this man. He comes back later, and when he does, he settles the argument.

Because notice what that tells you. Nobody at Ghazna had been overwhelmed by the beauty of Persian poetry. The court was running both languages side by side — a review treats the bilingual chancery under Mahmud's son Mas'ud as the moment New Persian had reached full parity with Arabic in affairs of state. Both were on the shelf. Which one got used came down to who was holding the post.

Which opens a question: if an empire adopts this language because of a staffing gap, then what is actually being bought here?

Now the part that genuinely should not make sense.

Move west, two generations on. The Seljuks tear into Anatolia and take it off the Byzantines — brand new ground, nobody's inherited bureaucracy. Their own language is Turkic. The language on the ground is Greek. The language of the faith is Arabic. Three obvious options.

They designated Persian. The Seljuk rulers and their Anatolian branch installed it as the language of administration, and in Konya, their capital, Persian was the common tongue — that's the finding in several studies of Anatolian Seljuk administration. Conquerors in freshly taken land, using none of the three languages you'd expect.

And this is not an inference from poems. A paper published by the Turkish Historical Society describes surviving appointment documents from Alp Arslan — including one handing the governorship of Khwarazm to one of his sons. The paperwork by which a Seljuk sultan appointed his own child to a province is in Persian.

So by now it's not a favor to one vizier. It's how states get run. Which leaves one thing unexplained. How does a system this deeply installed ever get cancelled by a few lines on a page? Hold that.

And first: who turned this accident into something nobody could pull back out?

[CH04 | 7:30–9:50 | 把上一章的偶然做成制度:给出一份把自己嵌进客户国家机器的动作清单,并交出第一组同口径的扩张量级]

One man: Nizam al-Mulk.

He started under Chaghri Beg — one of the Seljuk founders. When Alp Arslan took power, Nizam al-Mulk became his vizier. Alp Arslan faced rivals. Nizam al-Mulk crushed them. The throne stabilized.

Then Alp Arslan died. Nizam al-Mulk picked Malikshah — Alp Arslan's son — and made sure he got the throne. Malikshah kept Nizam al-Mulk on as vizier. Total run: about thirty years — from 1063 to 1092. Scholars call him the chief architect of Seljuk administration.

He didn't just advise rulers. He built the bureaucratic structure they ruled through. Tax collection. Record keeping. Appointments. The whole apparatus. And the people staffing it — the Persian scribes, the Persian clerks — were bound to the Seljuk state. When the Seljuks expanded, those officials went with them. New territory meant new tax rolls, new courts, new administration. And all of it ran in Persian.

The Seljuks were the military. The Persian administrative class was the infrastructure.

So what happened? Wherever Seljuk power reached, Persian as an administrative language followed.

Take Anatolia. The Seljuks took it from the Byzantines starting in 1081. After that, Persian remained the official and administrative language there for over five centuries. In major cities, it was the working language. In the madrasas it was taught as a subject. In official correspondence, it was the preferred script.

In Konya — capital of the Rum Seljuks — Persian was the common administrative tongue. Not Turkish. Not Greek. Not Arabic. Persian.

This wasn't about one generation of rulers loving Persian poetry. This was structural. The bureaucracy was Persian-speaking. The tax system was Persian-speaking. Once it was installed, it didn't matter which sultan came next. The machinery kept running in the same language.

Which brings the count to: one region, five centuries, embedded in government training and official communication.

But Anatolia's just one stop. The question now is: how much further east could this system stretch?

[CH05 | 9:50–13:30 | 把覆盖量级连续升级到观众原以为不可能的程度,同时坦白主体自身的硬限定却给出继续扩张的反向结果,并回收开场那件物证、第一次正面触到片名]

The answer is: all the way across two continents — and through three completely different sets of clients.

Think about the layer your field uses every day but never builds. That's what we're talking about.

Now watch what happens when the clients change clothes but keep hiring the same scribes.

First stop: the steppe empires. In 1295, the Ilkhanate's Mahmud Ghazan converted to Islam. That move made Mongol rule acceptable to his Muslim subjects. He funded scholars. And under his sponsorship, Rashid al-Din Hamadani completed the first true world history, written in Persian. Same scribes. New empire.

Second stop: the Indian subcontinent. In 1206, the Delhi Sultanate made Persian the administrative language. When Bengal was conquered in 1203 or 1204, Persian was used for all administration, all literature, all economic records.

Then in 1556, Akbar took the throne. He reformed the currency. He changed the inscriptions on Bengal's coins from Arabic to Persian script. For the next two hundred years — from Akbar's accession to Mohammad Shah's death in 1749 — Mughal rule brought a unified official language, a unified administrative structure, and a unified coinage system to all of northern India.

And the Mughal Empire itself was founded by Persianized Turks from Central Asia. The people who built it had already been shaped by this administrative culture.

Third stop: even further out. In the Deccan, Persian remained the main language of administration, diplomacy, and record-keeping for centuries. Nobles were trained in three languages: Marathi for military and tax matters, Persian for diplomacy, Sanskrit for law and ritual.

And we have proof of just how far this system traveled. In a manuscript collection from the eighteenth century, there's a copy of a letter written in Persian to the king of France. It discusses the war against the British in India. A letter from one side of the world to the other, written in a language whose homeland hadn't controlled an empire of its own in centuries.

So let's reset the count. From the eleventh century onward, New Persian was the written literary language of the court elite in nearly all non-Arabic-speaking regions of the northern and eastern Islamic world. That position lasted at least until the eighteenth century. It stretched from the Balkans under the Ottomans all the way to Bengal under the Mughals.

But here's what we have to be honest about. This entire sprawl was never a language that ordinary people spoke at home. It was a written language of courts and government offices. It lived in tax ledgers and royal decrees, not in marketplaces. The people who could read and write it were a specialized class whose job was administration.

And that specialization is exactly what made it expandable. A language that ordinary people speak spreads with migration and conquest. A language that only administrators use spreads with whoever hires administrators.

Which brings us back to that table in Calcutta. That law passed on June twentieth, eighteen thirty-seven. In effect December first. The one that said the government could waive the requirement that court and tax documents be written in Persian — and decide later which language would replace it.

What those two paragraphs cancelled wasn't just a foreign tongue. It was a language Indian offices had used for centuries. A language that had travelled from the Balkans to Bengal not because Iran won wars, but because people who did win wars needed someone to run the bureaucracy they'd just conquered.

And that's the first time the title starts to make sense. Persian wasn't really a Persian language. It was a bureaucratic infrastructure. A system empires rented when they didn't have one of their own.

But if it was that useful, if it kept expanding for centuries — then why did it disappear?

[CH06 | 13:30–15:00 | 用一句重定义把前面所有扩张的归因整体掀翻,在同一处集中收掉前面积压的几条悬念,再开出最后一条]

So what was Persian actually selling?

John Perry looked at the Ghaznavids, the Seljuks, the Ilkhanids, the Mughals. He said: when their empires expanded, written Persian expanded with them. The conquests weren't Persian conquests. The territory was someone else's victory. Persian was the hired help.

Now here's the part where everything you've heard gets flipped. There's a saying: "Everyone who conquered Persia eventually became Persian." It gets the direction backwards.

Remember that vizier in Ghazna who couldn't read Arabic? When he was replaced, Arabic came right back. That's not cultural magnetism. That's a job someone can be fired from.

The poet who saved the language with thirty years and fifty to sixty thousand couplets — he kept it alive. But what kept it employed from the Balkans to Bengal, across Anatolia for over five centuries — that wasn't poetry. That was administrative capacity someone didn't want to build themselves.

Persian wasn't spreading because Iran kept winning. It was spreading because the people who did win needed accountants.

The Iranian plateau had no Persian empire of its own for most of those centuries. But written Persian had its widest reach. The Seljuks brought it to Anatolia after taking the land from Byzantium. The Mughals brought it to Bengal. The Ilkhanids brought it into their administration. None of those were Persian armies. They were clients.

So the real business model wasn't representing a people. It was being the layer empires couldn't run without — and didn't want to build.

That's the answer. A country that kept losing wars still had its language spread to Bengal because the wars that mattered weren't its own. The conquerors weren't converting to a culture. They were hiring a system. And what got purchased was a skill set that could be dismissed.

Which brings us to the final question: if this system was that good, if it lasted that long — why did it end?

[CH07 | 15:00–17:25 | 主动把论点交给最不利的几条证据做压力测试,每条配一句不否认也不夸大的公允限定,论点不反转而是变窄变硬,并收掉一条早埋的悬念]

You've heard the version that makes it sound inevitable. But the version you heard isn't complete.

First: the coverage itself. From the eleventh century through the eighteenth, New Persian was the written literary language of courtly elites in nearly all non-Arabic-speaking regions of the northern and eastern Islamic world. Notice what that doesn't say. It doesn't say people spoke it at home. This was an office language.

Second: the retreat started long before the British showed up. By the early sixteenth century, rulers within the Persianate zone were already writing in their own tongues. But starting in the 1530s, Turkish pushed it out. The decline was already three hundred years old.

Third: that 1837 document. Act No. XXIX wasn't a command to switch to English. It was an authorization. It allowed the government to waive the requirement that documents be written in Persian — and the replacement language would be designated province by province. In Orissa, the Board of Revenue stopped using Persian in 1837. Immediately, officials started arguing over whether to switch to Bengali or Hindustani. The following year, several local languages received official recognition. What replaced Persian wasn't always English. Sometimes it was just whichever local language the government happened to pick.

Fourth: scholars reject the idea that you can blame it all on colonial policy. There's a volume published by Brill — one chapter argues the "language of rule" explanation is too simple. The chapter argues that Indo-Persian itself became aesthetically and intellectually conservative. That's the missing half. It didn't die because it lost a war. It had been losing ground for three centuries. When the British wrote those two paragraphs, they weren't killing a culture. They were canceling a contract. The contract could be canceled because what Persian sold was a service, not a root.

Which brings us to India. If the 1837 law was just the formal end — then who actually paid the cost when the office language changed?

[CH08 | 17:25–18:05 | 交出结局与代价账:把前面的制度性结论落到具体一群人身上,说明这个结局不可逆,收掉一条悬念并开出最后一条]

British India. Macaulay's memo laid the ground. Then came 1837. That two-paragraph act. December 1st, Persian out.

The clerks who ran the lower courts and tax offices. Muslims had held those positions through 1837 — because Persian was the language the system ran in.

For Hindu clerks who'd never used Persian at home, switching to English cost almost nothing. For the Muslim administrative class, it was a question of cultural identity. Their social and economic position collapsed.

Then 1844. Hardinge's order: government appointments depend only on knowledge of English.

The council records said it plainly: a sudden change would throw longtime servants into hardship. They knew. They went ahead anyway.

The system didn't lose a war. It lost the job. No daily speakers to fall back on. When the platform got swapped out, everyone standing on it went down with it.

So what can you take from this?

[CH09 | 18:05–18:48 | 把全片压成几条编号法则,每条配一句机理,再给一组同口径对照和一句可被复述的终极句,并开出最后一个开放问题]

And what it took to cancel: two paragraphs. Passed June 20, 1837. Effective December 1. The document said: "the language to be used shall be such as the government may from time to time determine."

It never won on its own. It won because someone else won and couldn't run the place without it. And when the client picks a different contractor — even one no better than you — the old one just stops getting called.

[CH10 | 18:48–19:00 | 用一个不作回答的开放问题把结论交回观众自己的处境,并回扣开场那件物证收尾]

Calcutta. That table with two paragraphs on it. "The language to be used shall be such as the government may from time to time determine."

Next time you see a contract that says "supplier to be designated by Party A," you'll remember. You're either the product, or you're the platform under it. And platforms don't get defeated. They get redesignated.
